articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited - The Guardian
articles.summary: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited  The GuardianHouthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say  BBCIran war updates: 58 recruits killed, 200 hurt in Houthi attacks in Yemen  Al JazeeraHouthi rebels strike Yemen’s government forces, killing at least 53  AP NewsHouthi attack kills 58 at Yemen government training camp, governor says  Reuters
articles.full_text:
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title: NATO reshapes military strategy amid warning of possible Russian attack by 2029 - ProtoThema English
articles.summary: NATO reshapes military strategy amid warning of possible Russian attack by 2029  ProtoThema English
articles.full_text:
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) will begin crucial negotiations in October to determine the forces and weapons systems allies will need to counter a potential Russian attack, as well as how to fund the new defence requirements. The alliance is preparing to redesign its military capabilities.
The talks will establish military capability targets for 2029, requiring each of NATO’s 32 member states to commit specific military forces and equipment.
The timeline is particularly significant because European officials have warned that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO member state by then.
At the same time, the administration of US President Donald Trump is considering a substantial reduction in America’s military presence in Europe. Such a decision could leave the alliance short not only of troops, but also of critical capabilities, including aerial refuelling aircraft, long-range missiles, and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets.
The forthcoming negotiations will test each country’s willingness to increase defence spending, whether Europe can meet a greater share of its defence needs without the United States, and whether NATO’s military plans should rely more heavily on emerging technologies such as robotics and artificial intelligence.
“It will be difficult,” a senior NATO diplomat told Politico, speaking anonymously because of the sensitivity of the issue. “Burden-sharing, the United States, how to reconcile the level of ambition with political priorities… It is a huge undertaking,” the diplomat added.
The process that will determine NATO’s military strength
Allies are expected to begin discussions in the coming days on the overall framework for the new targets, known as Political Guidance.
This is the first stage of a five-phase process called the NATO Defence Planning Process (NDPP). Through it, the alliance identifies the military capabilities it needs and then allocates specific commitments to member states.
French Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation and the official leading planning for the future conduct of warfare, stressed that the aim this time was not simply to repeat an established procedure. “The ambition is for this cycle to be a process of transformation, rather than something ready-made and taken off the shelf,” he said.
Politico spoke to 15 current and former NATO officials and diplomats, identifying five key issues expected to shape the negotiations.
1. How many troops and weapons does the alliance really need?
The first and most important issue is determining NATO’s so-called “level of ambition” — the number of troops and military capabilities that allies will commit to providing.
Traditionally, member states have agreed that, in addition to the forces required for major military operations, the alliance should maintain 18 additional brigades, each comprising around 5,000 troops. These forces are intended for smaller-scale crisis-management missions outside NATO territory, such as those carried out in Afghanistan or Kosovo.
However, US pressure on European allies to assume greater responsibility for their own security, under the approach known as “NATO 3.0”, could lead to these requirements being reconsidered. A substantial reduction or even the complete removal of provisions for such smaller-scale military operations could be on the table.
At the same time, allies will consider whether the defence-planning process itself should be accelerated to keep pace with the exceptionally rapid rate of technological development on the battlefield. Artificial intelligence and ground-based robotic systems are already changing the nature of military operations, making faster adaptation of defence plans necessary.
Another issue will be how conventional military forces, such as infantry units and combat aircraft, can support nuclear-armed countries, including the United Kingdom and the United States.
Nassima Barrois, NATO’s director of nuclear policy, stressed that conventional military support capabilities were an integral part of the defence-planning process. “Conventional support capabilities are very much part of the NDPP process. This is one of the key messages we are emphasising ahead of the upcoming negotiations,” she said.
2. How will NATO fill the gap if the US pulls back?
The possibility of a reduced US military presence in Europe is one of the biggest sources of uncertainty.
The Pentagon is expected to complete its review of the deployment of US forces across Europe in December, just as NATO’s negotiations are under way.
Earlier this year, Washington had already withdrawn military assets from the pool of forces available to the alliance, including strategic bombers, fighter aircraft, drones, submarines and warships.
The forthcoming US review is causing concern among European allies because it could lead to further withdrawals of critical assets, such as heavy transport aircraft.
The fact that the review’s findings are expected midway through the negotiations could also delay the process.
Washington’s efforts to scale back its military presence in Europe will force allies to find ways to replace American capabilities. This will open a difficult debate over the fair distribution of financial and military burdens at a time when national budgets are under increasing pressure.
Camille Grand, head of the European aerospace, security and defence industries association ASD and a former senior NATO official, described the change. “Until recently, the whole NATO process worked like this: you calculated what the alliance needed and, when you found that you did not have everything, the United States filled the gaps,” he said, adding: “That is no longer the case.”
One proposal under consideration is to abandon strict requirements for specific weapons systems and replace them with operational objectives. For example, rather than requiring a country to possess a particular number of missiles, it could be tasked with neutralising Russian command centres.
This would give European allies greater flexibility, particularly those without access to US weapons systems such as Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Fabrice Pothier, a former NATO director of policy planning and current chief executive of the consultancy Rasmussen Global, believes alternatives are available. “We do not need thousands of Tomahawks. But we can have thousands of cheaper, low-cost alternatives,” he argued.
3. Geographic disagreements: Russia is not everyone’s only concern
NATO’s growing focus on the Russian threat could trigger fresh disagreements among member states, as some believe other serious security challenges also need attention.
Officially, the alliance adopts a “360-degree” security approach, under which it must address threats from every geographical direction. In practice, however, since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, NATO’s focus has shifted significantly towards eastern Europe.
Over the past year, attention has also increasingly turned to the north, with the creation of a mission in the Arctic, largely in response to pressure from Donald Trump over Greenland.
Some allies, however, want greater attention paid to NATO’s southern and south-eastern flanks. Their concerns include the presence of Russian mercenaries in Libya, the potential weaponisation of migration flows, increased submarine activity, and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
These differing priorities could complicate the allocation of military forces and financial resources.
“There is too much emphasis on the north,” one NATO diplomat said. “We need to redefine our priorities,” the diplomat added.
4. More drones or more tanks? The crucial question
One of the most important military dilemmas concerns the balance between emerging technologies and conventional weapons systems.
The war in Ukraine has demonstrated the decisive role of drones and autonomous systems, which are being used on a massive scale on the battlefield.
NATO must now decide whether to prioritise the development and procurement of more drones or continue investing at the same intensity in conventional equipment such as tanks and artillery.
Most member states have already drawn up plans to increase their use of unmanned systems. The United Kingdom announced this year that it would create a “hybrid fleet” relying heavily on autonomous assets, including Type 93 uncrewed underwater vehicles.
France has earmarked around €8.4 billion for drones and loitering munitions, while Germany plans to establish its first specialised unmanned-systems regiment over the coming year.
This shift is driven not only by technological advances but also by the demographic challenges facing Europe.
Difficulties recruiting new personnel into European armed forces are increasing the need to deploy autonomous systems. As Camille Grand explained: “One of the reasons pushing everyone towards more unmanned systems is that we have ageing societies. We have a manpower problem.”
At the same time, countries must find a way to keep pace with Russian technological advances without exhausting their national defence budgets.
Admiral Pierre Vandier said Russia produces nine million drones a year, a figure that, in his view, demands a “fairly radical effort” from the alliance. One solution he proposed was adopting a model of regular upgrades to military equipment, similar to a subscription service. Such a system would allow weapons systems to be continuously updated, reducing the risk of their becoming obsolete within a short period.
5. Lessons from Ukraine: What NATO should adopt — and what it should avoid

articles.title: Decoupling From the U.S. Is Awkward - The Atlantic
articles.summary: Decoupling From the U.S. Is Awkward  The Atlantic
articles.full_text:
Suddenly, Canada is in the middle of a defense boom. Like other NATO countries that have skimped on their armed forces for decades, Canada is trying to quickly build up its military in the face of both rising international-security threats and a White House that regularly treats friends like foes. In the absence of trustworthy American leadership, many allies are working to become more self-reliant. But this is easier said than done, especially for Canada, which has enmeshed its own self-defense with the U.S. military more than any other American ally.
Since 1957, when Canada and the United States established the North American Aerospace Defense Command to jointly defend the continent during the Cold War, the Canadian military has grown closer to America’s. The otherwise small and underfunded Canadian Armed Forces is structured to deploy alongside its U.S. counterparts and to interoperate seamlessly with them. This has allowed Canada to make valuable military contributions in both countries’ interest at relatively low cost.
Until Donald Trump’s return to the White House, few in Canada were worried about how deeply intertwined the two militaries had become. Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government had contracted for billions of dollars’ worth of American-made military capabilities, including new surveillance planes, the combat system on Canada’s new warships, and 88 F-35 fighter aircraft. These investments have spared Canada the cost of developing cutting-edge equipment and allowed Canadian forces to operate interchangeably with the U.S. military. As long as the United States remained a benign ally, Canada was getting a great deal.

articles.title: Massive Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg escalates US-NATO war against Russia - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: Massive Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg escalates US-NATO war against Russia  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
Ukraine attacked Russia with more than 1,000 drones overnight Saturday, in the largest bombardment of St. Petersburg since the Second World War. The attack, in which Russia’s Defense Ministry counted 1,015 drones across 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea, was one of the heaviest bombardments of Russian territory since the war began.
These strikes are directly funded by the NATO powers, which have provided Ukraine with over $100 billion in weapons, and are carried out on the basis of targeting data provided directly by their militaries.
The latest attack is a response by the NATO powers to the warning Russia gave European governments on September 30, that threats to Russia’s territorial integrity would be met with “the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons.”
Faced with this blunt warning that their actions risk triggering a nuclear war, the NATO powers are escalating. On October 12, General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s top commander in Europe, threatened to “break” the enemy’s “warfighting system,” including “anything and everything that supports, sustains, or controls that force.”
Under these conditions, there is a growing admission within the US and international media that NATO and Russia are entering a “world war.” In one of the foremost examples, the Financial Times published Saturday a column titled, “Are we sleepwalking into World War III?” by its chief foreign affairs commentator, Gideon Rachman. The title of his essay is taken from a 2012 book by Australian historian Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914, which provided an apologetic explanation for the policies of German and European imperialism.
According to Clark, the war was the unforeseen outcome of mistaken judgments. The governments of the time and their leaders were not guilty of planning and starting war to achieve geopolitical and economic objectives. This benign interpretation of the war was especially welcomed by the German government and media, which praised Clark’s work and turned him into an intellectual celebrity.
Building upon Clark’s metaphor, Rachman depicts the imperialist powers as similarly clueless about the consequences of their actions. He writes, “Regions and countries that have for decades taken peace for granted—western Europe, east Asia, the Gulf states—now have to wrestle with the prospect, or the reality, of war.” It has become “commonplace,” he notes, “for world leaders to speculate publicly about the outbreak of a third world war.”
Rachman, citing a quote attributed to Leon Trotsky, declares, “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you.”
But the US and European leaders are not political somnambulists who are “sleepwalking” into World War III. They have been marching toward it with eyes open since the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The first President Bush proclaimed a “new world order” on the eve of the 1991 Gulf War. That war was followed by the intervention in Somalia, the bombing of Bosnia and the 1999 war against Serbia, the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, the destruction of Libya, the proxy war in Syria and the US-backed Saudi war in Yemen.
Since 2022, these wars have merged into a single global conflagration. It includes the US-NATO war against Russia in Ukraine; the Israeli genocide in Gaza, armed and defended by Washington; the bombing of Iran in June 2025; and the war against Iran launched on February 28 of this year.
The objective is the redivision of the world among the old imperialist powers. This violent and ongoing project includes the breakup of the existing Russian state, which will open up the vast Eurasian landmass to unfettered capitalist exploitation. For the oligarchs of finance capital, the loss of a few hundred million lives would be a small price to pay for this rich prize.
In Rachman’s telling, however, the danger of world war proceeds entirely from the actions of Russia and China. In this narrative, the threat of “world war” began with the decision Putin made in February 2022, with no antecedent history. Rachman asserts that an inflection point was reached when “Putin launched his ‘special military operation.’ In that time, the global political atmosphere has been transformed.”
The Russian invasion of Ukraine did not come out of nowhere. It was a reactionary and desperate response by the Russian capitalist oligarchy to years of provocations by NATO. NATO’s own leadership has said as much. In an interview published by the Washington Post in May 2023, then-NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg declared that the war “didn’t start in 2022. The war started in 2014.”
Stoltenberg continued, “And since then, NATO has implemented the biggest reinforcement of our collective defense since the end of the Cold War ... Until 2014, NATO allies were reducing defense budgets. Since 2014, all allies across Europe and Canada have significantly increased their defense spending ... this is a huge transformation of NATO that started in 2014.”
In 2014, the United States funded, armed and supported the coup that overthrew the pro-Russian government of Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych and installed the present regime, a dictatorship ruling under martial law. Since then the United States and NATO, as Stoltenberg explained, surged money and weapons to Ukraine, turning it into a frontline state for war against Russia.
But the Maidan coup was itself an outcome of decades of imperialist policy that had pushed the boundaries of the NATO alliance to Russia’s doorstep.
Rachman correctly centers the driving force of the eruption of global war in “a shift in the global balance of power.” He notes that, “In 1989, the year of the fall of the Berlin Wall, the G7 nations—the US, UK, Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan—accounted for around two-thirds of global economic output ... By 2022, the G7 represented about 43 percent of global GDP.”
This shift, according to Rachman, is “encouraging revisionist powers to challenge the global dominance of the US and its allies.” China’s share of world output rose from under 2 percent in 1989 to about 17 percent in 2024, according to World Bank figures.
However, by 2022, Rachman notes, the G7 still accounted for “about half of global military spending.” The old imperialist powers retain a military superiority they no longer possess economically. It is they, not China, that have spent the past 35 years at war, seeking to reverse by force what they are losing in the world economy.
The most bizarre element of Rachman’s column is his effort to blame the reemergence of global war on the public’s opposition to it. He writes that “the growth of anti-war sentiment in the US” has “created an opening for revisionist powers,” that US President Donald Trump “is clearly attracted to the idea that the US should retreat from its security commitments to its allies” and that “the greatest risk of a third world war may lie in that very uncertainty.”
Beset by an all-pervasive capitalist crisis and the growth of working class opposition, the imperialist powers seek through war a way out of their problems. The global eruption of imperialist war is only intensifying the class struggle and the capitalist crisis. It is driving workers and youth into struggle around the world, from the United States to France—where students and workers filled the streets this week against a government that has billions for rearmament and nothing for social needs.
The working class and youth must reject and oppose the insane imperialist militarism that is inciting global conflict and threatening humanity with a nuclear conflagration.

North Korean dictator Kim Jong-Un has sparked death rumours after failing to appear in public for a week. Unverified reports on social media suggest Kim was rushed to a Chinese hospital for urgent treatment after suffering a brain haemorrhage.
It was suggested that he was removed from the country because of the poor medical facilities in Pyongyang. The despot was last seen touring a defence museum in the North Korean capital on October 11. Wanjun Xie, chairman of the China Democracy Party, was among those feeding the discourse on X.
He wrote: "It is rumoured that recently, Kim Jong-Un ... suffered a severe cerebral haemorrhage and fell into a coma. Although a team of medical experts from Peking Union Medical College Hospital was dispatched to North Korea to assist in his treatment, the poor medical conditions in North Korea forced Kim Jong-Un to be transferred to Peking Union Medical College for emergency treatment."
He then went even further, suggesting the dictator had "succumbed to his injuries and died ... due to the severity of his condition". Another user added: "His body is currently being secretly transported back to North Korea without public announcement."
It's not the first time Kim has been the subject of death rumours, with similar speculation arising in 2020 after he failed to appear in public for several months. The recent rumours follow reports that he is "extremely obese", weighing more than 140kg and putting him at serious risk of cardiovascular disease, according to South Korea's National Intelligence service.
In the event of Kim's death, it is thought his younger sister Kim Yo-jong, 38, would take the reins of the nuclear-armed regime. While not much is known about her, Ms Kim has attracted international attention for insulting other foreign leaders, including telling former South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol to "shut his mouth" and calling him "really simple and childish". She also labelled former US president Joe Biden an "old man with no future" after he increased American support for South Korea in 2023.
Kim's sister would reportedly take control for an interim period until his daughter, 13-year-old Kim Ju-ae, is old enough to succeed him. The teenager has accompanied her father on a number of high-profile outings, including a state visit to China last year.
A source told The Sun she could oversee an even more formidable regime than her father. They said: "When we think about her upbringing and training to be a core North Korean elite, then we know from her father and grandfather that she will be playing the bloodsport of politics. That will require her to cashier disloyal aides through violent means. It's a job requirement for the leader."
Kim's reign is known for its brutal political purges and executions, ordering the deaths of hundreds of government and military officials to consolidate power, including his uncle, Chang Song-thaek in 2013. Agents also assassinated his half-brother Kim Jong Nam using a toxic nerve agent in Malaysia in 2017, and public executions, often by firing squad, are a common occurrence.

We're now down to about 12,000 nuclear weapons held by nine different nations, most of those held by the United States and Russia. And that's the lowest we've been since the 1950s, but 12,000 nuclear weapons is still a lot. And we're still locked in the struggle between those who think that these are terrible weapons that could end human civilization in a few minutes, and those who think that these are essential weapons for their national security.

And in fact, after the Second World War, we did enter something of a period of hard-won global consensus, right? Over the dangers of nuclear Armageddon, which gave rise to a number of global treaties. Right? Can you just very briefly walk us through kind of the important highlights of that history?

articles.title: Why does Lavrov say Trump's Gaza peace plan remains unimplemented despite ceasefire efforts? - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Why does Lavrov say Trump's Gaza peace plan remains unimplemented despite ceasefire efforts?  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has criticised the implementation of US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace initiative, saying the plan remains “just ink on paper” and that its underlying principles have not been respected. The remarks, attributed to Lavrov, raise questions about the progress of the US-backed framework for ending the Gaza conflict, although the date and venue of the statement could not be independently confirmed from an official transcript.
Lavrov's reported comments focus on the gap between the plan's stated objectives and its implementation. The framework envisages a ceasefire, the release of hostages, humanitarian assistance, reconstruction and transitional governance in Gaza. However, the precise commitments Lavrov was referring to were not specified in the available remarks.
Trump's comprehensive plan received backing from the United Nations Security Council through Resolution 2803, adopted on November 17, 2025. The resolution endorsed the framework and called on all parties to implement it fully and in good faith, while supporting transitional arrangements for Gaza's administration and reconstruction.
Implementation has faced significant obstacles. In a report submitted to the Security Council on May 15, 2026, the Board of Peace said the ceasefire had largely held despite continuing violations, but negotiations on the next stages of the plan remained unfinished. The report identified disagreements over the disarmament of Hamas, security arrangements and the transition to civilian administration as major challenges.
The United Nations also reported in September 2026 that the ceasefire remained fragile, Israeli strikes continued and the disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups had not been implemented. Transitional arrangements had been established but were not yet operating inside Gaza, while large-scale recovery and reconstruction remained limited.
These unresolved issues matter because the plan links security arrangements to the next stages of reconstruction and governance. Progress on disarmament, Israeli military withdrawal, humanitarian access and the establishment of a functioning Palestinian administration will influence whether the ceasefire can develop into a more durable settlement.
Lavrov's reported criticism also reflects Moscow's broader diplomatic interest in the Middle East and its calls for political solutions to regional conflicts. However, the remarks alone do not establish that Russia has proposed a new mechanism or that any party has formally withdrawn from the existing framework.
The next steps will depend on renewed negotiations involving the United States, regional mediators, Israel and Palestinian representatives. Egypt, Qatar and Türkiye have played key roles in mediation, alongside Washington. Further diplomatic consultations and progress on security and governance arrangements will be important indicators of whether the plan can advance beyond its current implementation difficulties.
Key highlights
- Lavrov criticises implementation of Trump's Gaza peace initiative.
- Russia says the plan's principles have not been respected.
- UN Security Council endorsed the framework in November 2025.
- Disagreements over disarmament and governance continue to delay progress.
- Regional mediators remain central to efforts toward implementation.

articles.title: Russia–Ukraine: Peace For Show, War As Usual – OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Russia–Ukraine: Peace For Show, War As Usual – OpEd  Eurasia Review

Key Takeaways:
- Efforts by President Trump and other actors including Turkey, Egypt, and India to secure an energy ceasefire have failed, with Ukraine—backed by the EU, UK, and Canada—rejecting demands to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
- Nearly five years into the war, Russia has not achieved its strategic objectives; its attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure are assessed as unlikely to produce decisive military gains, while Ukrainian strikes continue to degrade Russian refining capacity.
- The article expects intensified diplomatic initiatives, including possible U.S. pressure for a Putin–Zelensky meeting at the G20 in Miami, but anticipates that mutual energy strikes will continue, the front line will see only minor changes, and civilian suffering will not compel a settlement.
US President Donald Trump’s efforts to pressure Russia and Ukraine into agreeing to an energy ceasefire have failed. Attempts by other global actors, including Turkey, Egypt, and India, to persuade Moscow and Kyiv to reduce hostilities have also proved fruitless. What lies ahead for the two adversaries in the coming period?
Firmly backed by the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada, and several other Western allies, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has openly rejected Trump’s demand that Kyiv halt strikes on Russian oil refineries. Despite reports that Elon Musk, a close ally of the US president, has proposed restricting Starlink access in Ukraine, Kyiv remains determined to resist pressure from Washington to reach a deal that could serve Moscow’s interests.
Policymakers in Ukraine are fully aware that even if the US severely limits its aid to Ukraine, such a move is unlikely to have a decisive effect on the battlefield situation. The reason for their apparent lack of concern lies not only in Europe’s continued support for Kyiv, but also in the approach the Kremlin has taken to the war in Ukraine.
Nearly five years after launching its invasion, Moscow remains far from achieving its strategic objectives in Ukraine. Russia’s daily missile and drone strikes on shopping malls, residential neighborhoods, gas stations, and other civilian infrastructure across Ukraine have failed to deliver any decisive military advantage against the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The Kremlin’s ongoing campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, particularly power transformers at electricity substations, is undoubtedly intended to inflict severe hardship on the civilian population, but is unlikely to have any decisive impact on the Ukrainian military’s operational capabilities. To make significant gains in Ukraine, Moscow would first need to fundamentally change its military and political approach to the conflict – something that does not seem particularly plausible at this point.
Even Russia’s recent attempts to damage bridges in Kyiv seem to have been more a “demonstration of force” than a serious effort to disrupt Ukrainian military logistics. Ukraine, on the other hand, remains determined, despite Trump’s warnings, to knock out Russian oil refineries, knowing that such strikes could have far-reaching consequences for the Russian economy.
That, however, does not mean that Russia’s overall situation is catastrophic, at least for the time being. The very fact that the Kremlin was willing to reach a diesel deal with Washington suggests that some of Russia’s oil-refining capacity remains intact. Moreover, Moscow continues to export crude oil to its largest buyers, including China and India, generating a steady stream of revenue for the Russian budget.
However, in the long term, the ease with which Ukraine damages, if not completely destroys, Russian energy infrastructure and logistics facilities makes the current situation unsustainable for Moscow. Faced with this reality, the Kremlin seems to be looking for a way to, if not end the conflict, at least freeze it on terms that would allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to save face. But that is easier said than done.
Efforts by Trump and other international actors to broker a ceasefire were publicly welcomed by senior Russian officials. For Moscow, however, accepting a freeze in the conflict under the current circumstances would mean giving Ukraine time to rearm, regroup, and prepare for renewed fighting. That is why Russian officials repeatedly emphasize that they are seeking “a sustainable and just peace” rather than a mere truce.
Although foreign actors are undoubtedly aware of these realities, their repeated ceasefire and peace initiatives help them achieve at least two objectives: strengthening their standing on the international stage by portraying themselves as “peacemakers” and boosting their leaders’ approval ratings at home. Thus, as drone and missile strikes in Ukraine and Russia intensify, international players are expected to step up their diplomatic efforts to bring Moscow and Kyiv to the negotiating table.
In the coming weeks, Trump is likely to step up pressure on Putin to attend the G20 summit in Miami in mid-December and meet with Zelensky on the sidelines, despite the Kremlin having dismissed the prospect of such a meeting as “impossible.” Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine will almost certainly continue striking each other’s energy facilities, while the overall situation along the frontline will remain largely unchanged, with only minor tactical gains that are unlikely to have a significant impact on the outcome of the war.
Civilians on both sides, however, will continue to suffer, particularly during the winter months. Yet in wars – which, as the famous Prussian military theorist Carl von Clausewitz argued, are a continuation of politics by other means – civilian suffering is often treated as collateral damage or used as an instrument of pressure against the adversary. Therefore, in the present climate, no humanitarian tragedy is likely to compel Moscow and Kyiv to bring the conflict to an end.

A Conversation with Martha Turnbull of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats
In this IWI Emerging Technology conversation, Jeff Szuchman and Aidan Harte speak with Martha Turnbull of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats about how governments and societies are responding to information manipulation and other hybrid threats. They discuss why terminology matters, how China and Russia are using AI in influence operations, the difficulty of measuring the impact of information campaigns, attribution and deterrence, and how hostile actors learn from and cooperate with one another. The conversation also looks ahead to AI-enabled micro-targeting, the growing use of non-state proxies, and the long-term effects of foreign interference on trust in democratic institutions.
Note: This transcript has been edited for readability while preserving the meaning and substance of the conversation.
Transcript
Jeff Szuchman: Hello, and welcome to the Irregular Warfare Initiative’s Emerging Technology Series. My name is Jeff Szuchman. I’m the co-director of IWI’s Emerging Technology Program.
Aidan Harte: I’m Aidan Harte, advisor at the IWI Emerging Technology Program. Today, we’re joined by Martha Turnbull, director of the Community of Interest on Hybrid Influence at the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats in Helsinki.
Jeff: Hybrid CoE is an international expert organization that brings together 35 participating states and works closely with the European Union and NATO to understand and counter hybrid threats, from information manipulation and election interference to proxies, sabotage and other forms of coercion below the threshold of conventional conflict.
Aidan: Martha’s portfolio includes disinformation, AI, election interference, and proxies. She came to the role after 15 years in the UK government, working on national security issues including hybrid threats and counterterrorism.
Martha, welcome. Thank you so much for joining us today.
Martha Turnbull: Thank you for having me.
Jeff: So, Martha, we’re excited for this conversation. There’s a lot to cover, but let’s start with you and your story: how you came to this world of hybrid influence, and then also about Hybrid CoE and how that began. What was it that Hybrid CoE thought were issues that weren’t being addressed by governments and multilaterals?
Martha: Sure. So, from my perspective, I’ve spent over 15 years now working in the UK government. Initially, the first 12 or so years of my career were focused on counterterrorism. But I think, as anybody who works in the national security community can tell you, the direction of travel seemed to be very firmly towards hybrid threats or state threats.
And so there was a pivot in my career about three or four years ago, where I started looking at this problem increasingly, first from the lens of how counterterrorism and our responses to countering terrorism can help us deal with these emerging hybrid threats.
But then, more recently, as you say, I’ve moved to the Hybrid CoE in Helsinki, where I’m now one of the directors of a team of analysts working on a variety of different topics.
So really, for me, it’s been a fantastic continuation of my career. I’ve been an analyst for the majority of my career, so looking at deep dives into terrorist organizations and how they operate, but now thinking about hybrid threats, which are very different to that but, in my view, quite connected. And some of the responses are connected as well.
So it’s been helpful to have two different thematics throughout my career.
Aidan: Great. You know, one of the joys of being a part of IWI is getting to levy questions, I guess, that we would often get asked to answer.
So I wanted to sort of introduce this as well with a question about terminology—a definitional question—not just because there seem to be so many terms for similar ideas, but because the choices about which terms to use shape both organizational power dynamics and, certainly as we’ve seen in the U.S., can really influence funding.
Cognitive warfare is a common term in the irregular warfare community, but other terms are sometimes used to mean similar or the same thing, including foreign information manipulation and interference, active measures, mis- and disinformation, and others. I’ve often preferred, for example, the use of the term “malign narratives” over “disinformation” to avoid rejecting underlying grievances.
And so I’m really curious how you and Hybrid CoE think about the choices you make about terminology, and why do you think they matter?
Martha: Yeah, so I think terminology is really important. I think it can often be quite a thorny question because terminology is never neutral. And I think, particularly in this space, we can see how different terms emphasize different aspects of the problem.
So you’re right. In the work that I’m doing at the Hybrid Influence team at the Hybrid CoE, we work with participating states that call it disinformation. We work with other states who prefer to use the terminology FIMI—foreign information manipulation and interference. But we also have separate programs of work that look at cognitive warfare as a separate subset.
But we’re also constantly coming up against misinformation as well, increasingly fake news, which is kind of associated in this space. But also what we’ve seen recently is a trend towards using the term DIMI, which is domestic information manipulation and interference.
So you have all of these terminologies which are kind of just constantly floating around in this space. And which one is the best one, I think, often depends on the country or the organization and the context, and what works best for them.
But I think some of the key differences are important to recognize here, because when we talk about disinformation, we’re talking about false or misleading information. When we talk about FIMI, we’re focusing on the behavior of the actor behind the activity rather than the truthfulness necessarily of the individual pieces of content.
So this is about information manipulation and interference by a foreign actor, and so it’s quite specific in that way.
And then, obviously, at the Hybrid CoE, we look beyond this topic as well. We look at hybrid threats, which is obviously a much broader topic that includes information operations, but also includes that link across to cyber activity and other threats like economic coercion, sabotage, proxies, political interference. All of that kind of sits within that hybrid threats terminology.
So I think the conversation on this seems to be evolving. Certainly in the European Union context, countries within the European Union seem to be favoring FIMI because it allows countries to focus on the foreign element of that.
At the Hybrid CoE, we prefer to use disinformation because we’re more specifically talking about false and misleading information, so that helps us. But we also find that that enables us to have a conversation about foreign actors and domestic actors, including the ways in which they work together.
Whereas when you use FIMI, you’re talking specifically about the foreign actors. So that’s important.
And I think the other thing to mention in this space is that, when we are doing our analysis on disinformation, the work that kind of constantly comes up again is that the actors that we’re analyzing here are exploiting real grievances, often genuine societal debates or existing divisions within society.
And so it’s not always a question of, “Is the statement true or false?” but it’s about how it’s being manipulated. So it’s quite important to remember that as well when we’re thinking about this.
But I think the terminology is important because it can shape the policy responses. So, for example, if we just saw a problem as being misinformation, we might just focus on fact-checking because we’re talking about false information.
If we are just thinking about foreign interference, we’d be perhaps immediately looking at attribution, networks, financing, proxies, strategic intent—all of those things. And so that’s why the terminology can be really important, because it can shape the policy response that you have.
Aidan: I think that’s a fantastic response and very, very true. I think that nuance there is incredibly important because the terms that we use oftentimes inherently dismiss the legitimacy of a grievance or our ability to understand how to respond to it. So I really appreciate those distinctions. Thanks.
Jeff: Have you seen instances where there is disagreement about terminology kind of leading to real differences around policy responses that make it more difficult to cooperate?
Martha: So I think the only thing that we have seen in this space is that, in some states, their legislation makes it difficult for them to focus on foreign and domestic actors at the same time.
So they might be mandated to only do foreign actors, or they’re mandated to only do domestic actors. And so the piece that can sometimes be missing in that case is the way in which the two are often connected, and increasingly connected.
So I’d say that really is the problem. It’s less about terminology, but it’s more about, I guess, legislative structures and cooperation between departments and what is allowed and not allowed in certain circumstances within countries. That is the thing that stands out to me in that space.

Washington has taken the rare measure to issue a red alert to US citizens in 12 countries across the Middle East, citing risks of potential attacks on US interests.
US embassies across the entire Middle East issued identical security alerts on Monday, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran to exercise heightened vigilance.
The alerts warn all US citizens of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions due to the risk of military escalation linked to Yemen’s Houthis and Iran.
The warning covering 12 countries states that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area” and to “develop contingency plans in advance.”
“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions,” the alert said.
In Saudi Arabia, the embassy warned of a “complex security environment,” as “Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.”
The alert also states that “Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions.”
In Qatar, the US embassy urged its citizens on Sunday to monitor official alerts and local media, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and follow instructions from local authorities.
Qatar Airways announced on Monday that it will suspend its Saudi-bound flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until 24 October and reduce flights to Jeddah from seven to four per day.

Etihad Airways has extended cancellations between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until Saturday, October 24, citing regional disruption.

Iran reiterated its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, Reuters reported.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the proposal remained available despite stalled negotiations.
Tehran's demands include lifting the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, removing sanctions on Iranian oil exports and ending regional hostilities.
Washington, however, continues to insist that negotiations address Iran's nuclear programme.
The disagreement leaves uncertainty over when normal commercial shipping could resume through a waterway that previously carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade.
Egypt has offered Saudi Arabia military support against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, potentially widening the regional conflict.
Reuters reported that President Abdel Fattah Al Sisi requested an urgent parliamentary session to authorise assistance if Saudi Arabia seeks Egyptian support.
Discussions were expected to continue Monday.
The announcement follows repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure.

US West Texas Intermediate declined to $99.46.

According to the Emirates News Agency, discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation, regional security and efforts to achieve lasting peace.

No new UAE-wide restrictions on residents' daily activities were announced in the official statements reviewed. Residents should continue following government announcements and airline advisories.

articles.full_text:
Iran has signaled that it is preparing for another round of war with the United States and has issued public threats against Washington and its allies in an apparent bid to deter President Donald Trump from restarting the current conflict.
Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built large stockpiles of new weapons ready to be unleashed on targets beyond the region should the US resume hostilities that began in February.
Iranian officials have threatened to broaden their targets if the conflict resumes, floating options that include cutting undersea internet cables, striking AI data centers, and attacking regional oil and gas facilities.
“The world will be amazed,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said late last month. “We have new targets that have not yet been attacked,” he added.
Nearly nine months after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, the conflict has stagnated into a stalemate that has left everyone uncertain about Trump’s endgame and the world grappling with economic unrest. Both sides have claimed victory – Tehran pointing to its survival and Washington the damage inflicted on the Iranian regime. Meanwhile, the Trump administration continues testing new economic and military measures to force Iran into capitulation, which Tehran has stubbornly resisted.
“The war is not over,” Mohebbi said. “The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has prepared itself for a long-term war.”
Bracing for war
While Iran’s commanders signal strength and readiness, ordinary Iranians, long burdened by conflict and economic uncertainty, are once again bracing for the on the ground realities of war.
“Every single day and every night, we’re waiting for the bombing to start again,” a 70-year-old Tehran resident told CNN last week. “I’ve charged all my power banks, stocked up on water, and got everything ready, because the attacks could start again at any moment, any day.”
A mother of two described to CNN the fear she lives with as she sends her children to school each morning, past streets where Revolutionary Guards are visible, and military bases remain active.
“I would like to know exactly what else the US is planning to bomb?” she said. “They couldn’t even take (the Iranian leadership) out. You couldn’t negotiate either. So, what’s the point of starting another war?”
Iranians are “convinced” war is going to restart, another resident in Tehran told CNN.
“It’s all anyone can talk about…you just have it in the back of your head, is tonight the night? Is it tomorrow? I think it makes it worse that there areall this conversation about it, you can’t even take a break,” the resident told CNN.
The Iranians spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity in order to speak freely about their fears of further war.
Targeting Europe
Over the last few weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterm elections, several advisers told CNN privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before election day on November 3.
The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal and would mark a notable escalation.
“These are propaganda tools intended to intimidate the Iranian people,” Alireza Sheikh, an Iranian army commander said on Saturday. “The Iranian people are the father of all bombs.”
Iran has signaled a new, more offensive military doctrine that suggests it will not wait to be struck and could even launch pre-emptive strikes. Last week, Revolutionary Guards social media accounts reported that Iran conducted military exercises across the country, including launching 30 ballistic missiles in one go.
Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with The Washington Institute think tank focused on US foreign policy in the region, said if an emboldened Tehran decided to try its new long-range missiles against Europe in an attack, targets might include US forces based at airbases in England, or the logistic hub in Ramstein, Germany, the largest US military installation outside of the US.
“However, Iran would likely reserve that possibility to a very top level of escalation,” Nadimi said.
The US moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases earlier this month after an unspecified new threat, officials said. Days before the move, the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the US bombers had been stationed.
To increase their chances of hitting targets, Nadimi said Iran may potentially launch more sophisticated and coordinated swarms of AI-enabled drones fitted with cameras and datalinks that can communicate with each other, adjust flight paths and speed to evade jamming and air defenses.
“They haven’t demonstrated these capabilities yet, but they discussed developing such technologies in the past,” Nadimi said.
Iran may also seek to advance its cruise missile capabilities to include supersonic propulsion to better evade interception and try jamming military communication and surveillance satellites, he added.
Region prepared
Iranian commanders are preparing for what they regard as an inevitable resumption in hostilities, while also attempting to deter Washington by highlighting the costs of an attack, Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at International Crisis Group told CNN.
“Tehran wants to make clear that the next round will be fought on a much wider battlefield, with fewer restraints and potentially more lethal consequences,” Vaez said. “But the danger is that what Iran intends as deterrence could be interpreted in Washington as provocation, making the very war Tehran hopes to avert more likely.”
When the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, they killed the Islamic Republic’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei along with Iranian military commanders, top officials, and civilians, including schoolchildren. Iran’s retaliation focused mostly on its Arab neighbors, which it accuses of colluding with Washington.
Iran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the only maritime waterway used by neighboring nations to export oil, before striking civilian infrastructure across Arab cities. Dubai, a major tourist destination, was targeted, water plants in Kuwait were hit, and attacks on data centers disrupted banking services in several countries across the region.
Iran fired more than 2,500 missiles and drones on the United Arab Emirates alone, more than any other country, including Israel. Abu Dhabi intercepted nearly all of the projectiles, according to figures by the UAE’s defense ministry.
Last week, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, warned that Iran will target US assets in the region, including within the UAE, in retaliation for any fresh attacks
“If another war breaks out, numerous undersea cables, data centers, AI facilities and other infrastructure across the region could be destroyed,” Rezaei said.
A senior UAE official told journalists on Thursday that his country is better prepared should fighting resume.
“We don’t want war,” Ali Al-Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE’s Federal National Council said. “But if a war starts today, we are ready to deal with any threat that comes our way better than we were on February 28.”
“Whatever is needed to protect our national security, sovereignty and people, we will do it.”

articles.title: Egypt Says Ready to Back Saudi Arabia in War Against Iran-Allied Houthis - NTD News

articles.full_text:
CAIRO—Regional military power Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sent oil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.
Houthis Ramp Up Attacks on Saudi Arabia
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.
Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.
Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country's national security.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Sisi became president a year later.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.
Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistan after it sought US President Donald Trump's help to fight the Houthis. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.
The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu escalated threats against Iran on Sunday, and Tehran warned of retaliation even as diplomatic efforts continued over the Strait of Hormuz and the wider conflict.
Trump warned that the United States could “soon finish the job” against Iran unless Tehran changed course, while giving Netanyahu his “complete and total endorsement” ahead of Israel’s October 27 election.
“They have been systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump suggested Washington could take on the fight itself if Netanyahu failed to remain in power, saying that with the “wrong Leader” in Israel, “America will have to do this work ourselves.”
In a briefing with Israeli journalists on Sunday, Netanyahu said bringing down the Islamic Republic remained a key Israeli objective and that he had directed the country's security agencies to pursue it.
Netanyahu said 90% of the work required to defeat Israel's enemies had been completed, while pointing to Iran's economic crisis and protests as signs of what he described as the government's weakness.
“We must bring this regime down once and for all,” Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was prepared to act independently of Washington if necessary.
Responding later to Trump's endorsement, Netanyahu said: “Together we will complete the mission!”
Tehran answers threats
Iranian officials responded with a series of warnings against renewed US or Israeli military action.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi directly challenged Trump's “finish the job” language, saying Iran had emerged stronger from the previous confrontation.
“Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” Araghchi wrote on X.
He also accused Netanyahu of seeking to draw the United States into another war to advance his own political interests.
Iran's parliament also approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as defense minister on Sunday, putting a veteran of the country's missile and aerospace industries in charge of its defense apparatus.
Akhlaghi warned Trump against another US attack, saying Washington should instead focus on getting its forces out of the region safely.
Other Iranian military officials issued similar warnings. Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi said another attack would draw a response “different from, and more severe than before,” while an IRGC spokesman threatened a devastating response against Israel if Iran's energy infrastructure were targeted.
Diplomacy remains on table
Despite the escalating rhetoric, Tehran said its proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting negotiations with Washington remained available.
Araghchi said Iran's seven-day proposal, first presented in September, remained on the table as Tehran reviewed Washington's response. Under the plan, the strait would reopen on the sixth day and negotiations would begin on the seventh if Washington accepted Iran's conditions.
Iran's conditions include lifting the US blockade on its ports, removing sanctions on oil exports and ending hostilities across regional fronts.
Washington, meanwhile, wants Iran to agree to significant reductions in uranium enrichment, while Tehran wants initial talks focused on restoring security and oil flows through the strait.
The Gulf Cooperation Council also pushed for a diplomatic solution on Sunday during a meeting of its foreign ministers in Bahrain.
The GCC condemned continued Iranian missile and drone attacks against its member states, demanded an immediate end to the attacks and called for the restoration of maritime security and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
The bloc also called for a return to dialogue and diplomacy, but said any understandings with Tehran should address Iran's nuclear and missile programs, drones and support for proxies, with GCC states involved in negotiations affecting their security.
Tensions persist at sea and across region
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said an oil tanker struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, causing an explosion and fire in its engine room. The Guards warned that vessels switching off their navigation systems while transiting the waterway would be classified as “hostile vessels.”
Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations said a southbound tug northeast of Khor Fakkan in the UAE was struck by two unknown projectiles, damaging the vessel and causing one minor casualty. The tug continued on its route.
The regional confrontation also continued around Saudi Arabia. The GCC condemned escalating Houthi attacks and reaffirmed its collective support for Riyadh.
Egypt said it was prepared to provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to Saudi Arabia. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi had sought parliamentary authorization on Saturday for the military to help defend the kingdom if Riyadh requested assistance.

articles.title: Helium is way more important than you might think. And the supply chain is in crisis. - CBS News
articles.summary: Helium is way more important than you might think. And the supply chain is in crisis.  CBS News60 Minutes Transcript: Helium in short supply as Iran war continues, with spot prices tripling  CBS NewsPreview: Helium Super Summit 2026  gasworldHow Impacted Is the Helium Market from the Hormuz Crisis?  Energy News BeatHelium Shortage Drives Prices Higher as Iran War Disrupts Supply  SuaraGarut.ID
articles.full_text:
The world's helium supply is facing a shortage seven months after Iranian strikes on a Qatari gas facility and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. A range of industries are feeling the impact with no end to the war in sight.
While most people associate helium with party balloons and squeaky voices, this finite and irreplaceable natural resource is critical for modern life. Without helium, there are no smartphones, cars, MRI machines, rocket launches, or missiles.
Helium is also challenging to extract and transport, according to Cliff Cain, the president of a helium exploration company. It needs to be kept at 452 degrees below zero Fahrenheit in transit. Once released into the atmosphere, that's it for helium – it's gone. Cain said he's spent decades warning that the complicated supply chain is vulnerable to disruption, with the helium supply concentrated in too few locations: Algeria, Poland, Russia, Qatar and the United States, with the bulk coming from the latter two countries.
"All it takes is a few of those to fall and the whole supply chain comes unraveled," he said.
What does the Iran war have to do with helium?
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February trapped one-third of the global helium supply in the Persian Gulf. Then, , the facility that produces all that helium in Qatar, was hit by Iranian strikes in March, further rattling supply chains.
Ras Laffan is the world's largest facility for natural gas, and its byproduct, helium. After the strikes, the Qataris said it would take at least three years to get the facility back in full operation. Ras Laffan did not respond to requests for comment about the extent of the damage to the helium infrastructure specifically.
Qatar is the second largest producer of commercial helium in the world after the U.S. Most of the U.S. helium comes from a single Wyoming facility, according to the Wyoming Energy Authority, and U.S. helium exports are up 70% since the war began, according to export data from the US Census Bureau.
But the U.S. can't offset the shortage indefinitely, and the longer the war with Iran continues, the tighter the global supply chain of helium gets. Spot prices on helium have tripled since the start of the war, according to Rich Brooke, a former executive at Air Liquide, one of the six major international helium suppliers.
Companies in South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore are now looking to the U.S. for helium, and it's not clear how long the U.S. can accommodate that demand. It depends on how long the war lasts. For now, some helium suppliers are drawing from their reserves, which are stored in deep, underground salt caverns.
"If you can tell me what's going to happen in the Strait of Hormuz between now and three months from now, I can tell you exactly what'll be happening in the helium business. Unfortunately, you can't, and so I can't," Brooke said.
Helium: More than something for balloons
With war ongoing, the Pentagon has asked some defense contractors to quadruple their production capacities of certain weapons. That worries Cliff Cain because helium is needed for weapons development, he says.
"You can't make modern warfare without helium. And that's just a fact," Cain said. "You've heard about the missiles, the hypersonics. Without helium, you can't make the fiber optics. You can't produce the munitions. You can't produce the electronics that goes on these things. And so if you don't have helium, your opportunity to make war becomes even more difficult."
The nonrenewable natural resource is also used in scientific research, including at Joe Sachleben's University of Chicago lab. The lab uses helium in nuclear magnetic resonance machines to develop breast cancer drugs, immunotherapies and treatments for Alzheimer's disease.
While helium is naturally a gas, it becomes a liquid if it gets cold enough — the coldest on Earth. Every couple of months, Sachleben pours 100 liters (roughly 26 gallons) of helium onto magnets in the lab to stabilize them at 452 degrees below zero.
"Once it gets to a critical level, we have to put helium back in the magnet to keep it cold," he said. "If that doesn't happen, we break the magnet"
There's no substitute, no work-around.
Helium is also critical for many electronics. One-fifth of the world's helium is consumed by the semiconductor industry, according to the Compressed Gas Association. Polar Semiconductors outside Minneapolis manufactures chips for car engine systems, servers in data centers and the U.S. military.
Around 40-50% of the machines in a fab, the ultra clean area where they manufacture the semiconductors, use helium in some way, according to Polar's President and COO Surya Iyer. Hundreds of steps in the process involve helium. No helium? Everything gets shut down.
The helium crisis is hitting at a time when Polar is planning to double production capacity to roughly 140 million chips a month.
"The AI data centers are growing [a] lot of demand for semiconductors. Electrification is growing demand for semiconductors," Iyer said. "And that means the demand for helium is going to be growing for a long time."
What's being done about the limited helium supplies
Polar is able to hedge its helium reserves by relying on three suppliers. Still, the company has felt the effects of the shortage. One of its suppliers has put them on allocation — essentially a rationing program.
Sachleben's supplier also hit his lab with the rationing plan.
"They basically have said, 'Well, we'll give you 50% of what you used last year.' That doesn't help us," Sachleben said. "And so what we have to do is decide which machines are we going to sacrifice and which one are we going to try to keep."
His lab found a backup supplier, but that supplier is unable to guarantee helium deliveries. Then last month, he got a message saying that supplier was about to run out. Sachleben said he's not feeling hopeful about getting the helium he needs as the war in Iran continues.
"I don't see an end to the current conflict," he said. "And even if we do have an end to the conflict, it'll take a while for the supply lines to get going again."
