articles.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world - BBC
articles.summary: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world  BBCEl Nino looms large over U.S. Winter Outlook  National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (.gov)Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?  The Economist‘Second Arm’ Super El Niño Surges Toward What Could Be the Strongest in 1,000 Years  SURFER MagazineA record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
- Published
El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.
Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.
The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.
Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world.
Indonesia battles worst wildfire season since 2015
Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El Niño years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015.
This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.
This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El Niño.
The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness.
More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.
East Pacific explodes with hurricane activity
In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far.
There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes.
This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.
Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.
Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.
The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño.
Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo.
Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month.
Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie.
Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.
Atlantic hurricane season remains eerily quiet
In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.
El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.
There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.
This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward).
Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.
In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point.
This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.
Reduced monsoon rain threatens agriculture in India
The drier and warmer theme has also taken hold in India, where the essential monsoon rainfall has been 13% below average.
While the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) would consider this still to be in the 'normal' range, the overall average doesn't reflect the variation in rainfall across India.
While Central India had around its normal expected rainfall, the east and north-east were around 26% drier than average and put into 'exceptional' drought. Southern states of India were 24% drier than average.
Even where rainfall was nearer to average, the rain did not fall continuously as is typical during the monsoon, instead flipping between long dry spells and extreme rainfall.
This adds more stress and vulnerability to agriculture yields.
India is influenced by a number of different weather patterns that can affect the monsoon season and so scientists suggest that El Niño may not have been the only factor.
Strong typhoons target east China and Japan
Further west in the Pacific, it's also been an active season in eastern China and Japan as storms including Maysak and Dujuan have brought recent widespread floods and landslides.
According to the Japanese Meteorological Agency, there have been 10 tropical cyclones forming in the western Pacific Ocean - the highest number in a season since 1966.
During El Niño the warmer Pacific brings changes to wind patterns, meaning cyclones tend to form further east, away from Japan and east China.
However, this means there is a bigger distance and more time where storms can feed off the warmer waters, gaining energy to become more intense typhoons before they hit land.
Scientists believe that additional typhoons are likely to develop this year with the potential for further impacts to Japan or east China.

articles.title: Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House  Al JazeeraTrump and Melania’s awkward speech on women’s health — and the comical hypocrisy behind it  The IndependentMelania Trump pushed Trump on women’s health overhaul | Exclusive  USA TodayTrump Belittles Melania to Her Face in Public Humiliation  The Daily BeastTrump signs order creating NIH division, task force for women's health  Reuters
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that will establish a dedicated women’s health division within the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as well as a White House task force focused on the subject.
During a signing ceremony in Washington on Monday, First Lady Melania Trump praised the initiative as setting “a new standard for women’s health in America”.
“This is a transformative moment for women in America. Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health,” she said.
“Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The newly minted project, spearheaded by the first lady, requires the new health division to be established within 90 days.
It aims to accelerate scientific discoveries, expand clinical access for women’s health and modernise care throughout every stage of a woman’s life.
The new division at the NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research, according to the White House.
Melania Trump gestured to “super intelligence, advanced biotechnology and groundbreaking therapies” as tools that offer a “unique chance to reinvent women’s healthcare”.
The first lady’s office has identified “five pillars” for innovation in the field. One involves funding targeted research to develop cures for diseases that affect women, such as endometriosis.
Another calls for a quicker timeline for “promising therapeutics” to reach female patients.
“In 2026, medical advances can do more than just prolong life,” said Melania Trump. “It should give women the freedom to live life to its fullest, to pursue our dreams, experience love, discover, create, travel and lead.”
The White House task force will be co-chaired by the newly cancer-free White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, as well as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
While Monday’s executive order mandates that the HHS must fund the administrative costs of the task force, the order itself does not include any specific funding targets or dollar amounts.
Experts have noted that Melania Trump has kept a relatively low profile during Trump’s second term.
Her public appearances have been fewer than during Trump’s first term, though she has stepped into the public spotlight to promote improvements to foster care and the role of technology, such as artificial intelligence in education.
During Trump’s first term, the first lady launched the “Be Best” campaign focused on child well-being, safe social media and countering opioid abuse.
But critics have questioned how effective Monday’s executive order might be, given the cuts Trump has made to the federal workforce since his second inauguration.
Thousands of employees have been laid off at the NIH alone, with Kaiser Health News reporting that its workforce is at its lowest level in decades.
The NIH was also given a deadline to slash spending by 35 percent across all of its divisions, amounting to a massive $2.6bn budget reduction.
In April 2025, the HHS drew widespread condemnation and a multi-state lawsuit after abruptly moving to terminate regional contracts for the Women’s Health Initiative, the nation’s largest longitudinal study on older women’s health at the time.
Critics warned that the move would jeopardise life-saving research on cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporotic fractures for senior women.

articles.title: Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France - Euronews
articles.summary: Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France  EuronewsCurfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France  BBCFrench riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates  POLITICO.euFrance protests: Curfews issued within several cities after violent riots - as Trump claims he warned Macron  Sky NewsIn pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters  BBC
articles.full_text:
Saturday’s violent protests and looting across France have deepened Macron’s political isolation, raising questions over his authority.
With only months left in his presidency, Emmanuel Macron faces mounting social unrest and political criticism that could ultimately shape his legacy.
After student protests over living conditions erupted into violence last Saturday, Macron has come under fire from across the political spectrum over his handling of the security situation and his response to grievances over education, the cost of living and inflation.
The unrest comes as France grapples with record public debt, soaring fuel prices and escalating international conflicts.
The Yellow Vests movement, which has helped coordinate the protests, announced a “second act” on Monday, with further demonstrations planned for next weekend.
Addressing the nation, Macron condemned violence and announced new operational procedures for security forces.
The Paris prosecutor’s office reported 855 arrests linked to the demonstrations, with 557 people placed in police custody, 433 of whom were adults, representing 78% of those detained.
“Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” Macron said. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”
The response is likely to add to the pressure on Macron, whose performance was viewed unfavourably by 82% of respondents in an Ipsos-BVA poll conducted in October.
The French president is currently on a diplomatic trip to the Gulf, which the Élysée says aims to secure energy supplies as prices rise. However, his decision to leave Paris amid the crisis has drawn criticism, with some accusing Macron of evading the situation.
Le Pen capitalises on chaos
Across the political spectrum, several potential presidential candidates have argued that Macron has lost authority and that his response came too late.
“We have the feeling that the government is collapsing under its own weight, that it is completely overwhelmed,” said Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, which is leading in polls ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election.
Speaking at a press conference at the party’s headquarters on Monday, Bardella pledged tough measures to restore order if the National Rally came to power. “France is caught in a vice between powerlessness and violence,” he said.
Polls put Marine Le Pen ahead of all her potential rivals in the 2027 presidential race. She faced Emmanuel Macron in the 2017 and 2022 run-offs, losing both times.
In the aftermath of the looting, Le Pen said France had been “ravaged” by “an alliance of criminals from the banlieues and politicised professional rioters”.
Le Pen is expected to focus her campaign on migration and law and order, issues that have traditionally resonated with far-right voters, while playing down foreign policy issues such as the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical tensions.
Macron faces criticism from former allies
Macron has also faced criticism from his former prime ministers, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both of whom are running in the 2027 presidential election.
Both are seeking to distance themselves from Macron and his political legacy.
“Like millions of French people, I would have preferred to see decisions and initiatives aimed at restoring order,” Philippe wrote on X.
Attal called on the state to employ all means "so justice is done" including AI facial recognition and deploying the army "if necessary". Macron did not announce extra security measures on Sunday, asking local authorities to coordinate with the police.
The divided French left, riven by internal tensions, accused the government of failing to protect citizens.
“This is unprecedented in its gravity,” Raphaël Glucksmann, a French MEP and social-democratic contender in the 2027 presidential election, told RTL radio. “I had the feeling that France was dissolving, that the Republic was disintegrating, that the state no longer existed.”
Bruno Retailleau, another presidential hopeful representing the conservative Les Républicains party, described Macron as “completely out of his depth, incapable of deploying the full force of the state against the chaos threatening the Republic”.
He cited the arson attack on Limoges town hall and vandalism at Marseille’s town hall.
Senior members of the government have also acknowledged shortcomings in the response.
Police fiasco
On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations. He offered to resign “because I felt responsible for everything that happened”, but Macron rejected his request.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin likewise acknowledged that the authorities had “undoubtedly failed” in their response, citing “shortcomings in intelligence gathering”.
Macron has found few defenders among his former allies, some of whom blame the current political turmoil on his decision to dissolve the National Assembly in June 2024. The move plunged France into political uncertainty, leaving successive governments exposed to the threat of no-confidence votes.
Beyond the immediate security crisis, commentators argue that Macron has alienated young people who helped propel him to power in 2017.
Some protesters have criticised his 2018 high school reforms, arguing that changes to the organisation of specialist subjects have led to longer school days.
In a recent opinion piece, Le Monde described Macron’s relationship with young people as a “major political failure”.
The article drew parallels with the Yellow Vests movement, which erupted in December 2018 amid widespread anger over purchasing power and the rising cost of living.
“Restoring public order is an essential prerequisite for beginning the talks promised on Sunday with all stakeholders and, in doing so, resuming a social dialogue that has been broken for far too long,” the piece concluded.

articles.title: Hormuz attacks overwhelm UKMTO - Splash247
articles.summary: Hormuz attacks overwhelm UKMTO  Splash247Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow  BBCTehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say  The Washington PostIran war updates: ‘Violating’ vessel on fire in Hormuz after sea mine blast  Al JazeeraWatch: Iranians recover new iPhones floating in Strait of Hormuz  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
The sheer volume of attacks on commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz has left Britain’s maritime security reporting centre struggling to keep track, with most vessels targeted in the increasingly dangerous waterway no longer reporting incidents directly.
UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) admitted in its latest weekly assessment that it is “struggling to accurately report true number of attacks”, warning that the majority of vessels attacked are refusing to report incidents. The organisation said it was aware of further attacks through other sources but could not include them in its figures without verification
UKMTO has recorded 135 incidents related to the Iran-US conflict since hostilities began on February 28, including 114 reports of vessel damage and 76 people killed or injured. Twelve attacks were recorded in its latest weekly assessment, ten in Hormuz itself, one in the Arabian Gulf and another in the Gulf of Oman. Of the vessels involved, one was lost, two were disabled and three had unconfirmed outcomes.
The violence has continued through the weekend, with attacks spreading well beyond the narrow confines of Hormuz.
On Friday, the 302,977 dwt VLCC ST3 was struck by an unidentified projectile approximately 68 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia. The Marshall Islands-flagged tanker suffered an engine room fire and lost power, according to maritime security firm Vanguard. All 15 Indian seafarers aboard were safely evacuated to a nearby UAE-flagged containership.
Later on Friday, another tanker was attacked approximately 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, this time by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat. The projectile damaged the vessel’s aft port quarter. All crewmembers were reported safe, although the full extent of the damage remains unclear.
Saturday brought further alarming claims from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which said two fully laden supertankers, each carrying more than 2m barrels of crude, had struck naval mines while attempting to transit Hormuz without Iranian authorisation. The IRGC claimed both vessels caught fire, with one suffering a major engine room explosion that left it immobilised. Neither ship has been identified and no independent confirmation has emerged. In its latest assessment, the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) explicitly stated that there was no substantiation for the Iranian claims.
On Sunday, a tug travelling south approximately 20 nautical miles northeast of Khorfakkan was struck by two unidentified projectiles. One crewmember sustained minor injuries and the tug suffered damage, although it was able to continue its voyage.
A further security incident was reported on Saturday in the Gulf of Aden, where an LNG carrier was approached by a skiff carrying seven people. Two shots were fired at the gas carrier before its armed security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to withdraw. Maritime authorities are treating that incident as suspected piracy rather than a confirmed Iranian attack.
Despite the extraordinary violence, oil continues to move. Signal Ocean data shows approximately 13.9m barrels per day of crude and another 2.3m barrels per day of oil products still passing through Hormuz.
Scandinavian bank SEB argued in a new report today that the disruption is “more a risk-premium story than a volume blockage”, with oil continuing to move through the shuttle system established to maintain exports.
The distinction between cargo volumes and vessel movements is significant. UKMTO’s latest figures show 254 vessel transits in a week, approximately 70% below pre-war levels. JMIC reported around 217 vessels waiting at anchor near Fujairah and Khorfakkan on Sunday, with congestion continuing to build outside the strait.

articles.title: "Universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable": India calls for legally binding framework for nuclear disarmament at UN - India's News.Net
articles.summary: "Universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable": India calls for legally binding framework for nuclear disarmament at UN  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
New York [US], October 20 (ANI): India has called for a universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable framework for nuclear disarmament at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) First Committee, stressing that decisions on the use of nuclear weapons must remain under human control amid the growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into defence systems.
Delivering India's official statement under the nuclear weapons cluster at the UNGA First Committee, Congress MP Manish Tewari highlighted the need to address technological and operational risks associated with nuclear arsenals, particularly those arising from the use of emerging technologies in nuclear command and control systems.
India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations highlighted Tewari's remarks in a post on X, reiterating New Delhi's commitment to global nuclear disarmament and efforts to strengthen the international non-proliferation regime.
'India acknowledges that the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear command and control raises real questions,' Tewari stated. 'We espouse the principle that the decision to use nuclear weapons should be taken by humans.'
Reaffirming India's foundational defence doctrine, the delegate noted that New Delhi's strategic capabilities are purely defensive and shaped by regional security realities rather than targeted at any single nation.
'As a responsible nuclear weapon state, India maintains a policy of credible minimum deterrence with a posture of no first use and non-use against non-nuclear weapon states,' Tewari declared. 'We are prepared to convert these undertakings into multilateral legal arrangements. I wish to underline that India's capabilities are shaped by our unique security environment and are not directed against any specific actor.'
Reiterating New Delhi's commitment to nuclear restraint, India reaffirmed its adherence to a voluntary unilateral moratorium on nuclear testing. Tewari also advocated for legally binding negative security assurances to protect non-nuclear nations.
'India believes that legally binding assurances to non-nuclear weapon states against the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons should alleviate their sense of insecurity, and thereby strengthen the non-proliferation regime,' he noted, adding that such guarantees would directly contribute to reducing nuclear risk worldwide.
Underlining India's long-standing position on complete global denuclearisation, Tewari reaffirmed that New Delhi remains steadfastly committed to 'nuclear disarmament that is universal, non-discriminatory, and verifiable.'
'This goal can be achieved by a step-by-step process underwritten by universal commitment to an agreed, non-discriminatory, multilateral framework,' Tewari explained. 'We outlined this approach in our 2006 working paper to the First Committee, and again in 2007 at the Conference on Disarmament as document CD/1816. The relevance of this approach endures.'
Tewari also highlighted two resolutions that India traditionally tables at the UN First Committee to promote nuclear disarmament and reduce the risks associated with nuclear weapons.
Reducing Nuclear Danger (Tabled since 1998): Draws attention to the hazardous 'hair-trigger alert status of nuclear weapons' and calls for urgent de-alerting and de-targeting to eliminate the risk of accidental or unintentional use.
Convention on the Prohibition of the Use of Nuclear Weapons (Tabled since 1992): Calls on the Conference on Disarmament to negotiate an international convention prohibiting the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons.
'Such a universal legally binding agreement would build the political will needed for the total elimination of nuclear weapons,' Tewari emphasised, soliciting continued co-sponsorship and support from UN member states.
Clarifying India's position on existing international treaties, the statement noted that while the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) does not impose legal obligations on New Delhi, India's broader commitment to global non-proliferation remains unchanged.
'The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons does not create obligations for India. Our commitment to global nuclear disarmament, nonetheless, remains unchanged, as does our commitment to strengthening non-proliferation,' Tewari affirmed.
Concluding the statement, Tewari stressed the importance of international cooperation to prevent terrorists and non-state actors from accessing nuclear weapons, materials and technology.
'We also remain committed to promoting international efforts to prevent terrorists and non-state actors from gaining access to nuclear weapons, materials, and technology,' the MP said. (ANI)

articles.title: NATO is being redesigned against the backdrop of a possible Russian attack by 2029! Five key issues that will determine its strength - Gazeta Express
articles.summary: NATO is being redesigned against the backdrop of a possible Russian attack by 2029! Five key issues that will determine its strength  Gazeta Express
articles.full_text:
Crucial negotiations to define the forces and weapons systems that allies will need to confront a possible Russian attack, as well as how to finance new defense requirements, will begin in October. NATO faces the challenge of reviewing its military power.
The talks will set military capability targets through 2029, obliging each of the Alliance's 32 member countries to make available concrete military forces and equipment.
This timeline takes on particular significance, as European officials have warned that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country by then.
At the same time, the Donald Trump administration is considering a significant reduction in the US military presence in Europe. Such a decision could leave the Alliance short not only of military personnel but also of essential capabilities, such as aerial refueling aircraft, long-range missiles and intelligence-gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance assets.
The upcoming negotiations will test each country's willingness to increase defense spending, Europe's ability to meet a greater share of its military needs without the US, and the question of whether NATO's military plans should rely more on new technologies, such as robotics and artificial intelligence.
“It will be difficult,” a senior NATO diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue, admitted to Politico.
"The burden-sharing, the United States, the way in which ambitious objectives will be combined with political priorities... It's a gigantic undertaking," he added.
The process that will determine NATO's military power
Allies are expected to begin discussions in the coming days on the general framework of new objectives, known as "Political Guidance".
This is the first step in a five-stage process, called the NATO Defence Planning Process (NDPP). Through it, the Alliance determines the military capabilities it needs and then assigns concrete obligations to member states.
French Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation and the leader of planning for how to conduct war in the future, stressed that this time the aim is not simply to repeat a routine procedure.
"The ambition is for this cycle to become a transformation process and not be something ready-made, taken off the shelf," he declared.
Politico spoke with 15 current and former NATO officials and diplomats, identifying five key issues expected to define the negotiations.
How many soldiers and how many weapons does the Alliance really need?
The first and most important issue is related to determining NATO's so-called "level of ambition," that is, the number of soldiers and military capabilities that allies will commit to making available.
Traditionally, member states have agreed that, in addition to the forces needed for major military operations, the Alliance should have 18 additional brigades, each with around 5.000 soldiers.
These forces are intended for more limited crisis management missions outside NATO territory, such as those conducted in Afghanistan or Kosovo.
However, US pressure for European allies to take on a greater share of responsibility for their own security, within the framework of the approach called "NATO 3.0", may lead to a revision of these demands.
In fact, the possibility of discussing a significant reduction or complete abolition of provisions for such smaller military operations is not ruled out.
In parallel, Allies will consider whether the defense planning process itself should be accelerated in the future, in order to adapt to the extremely rapid pace of technological developments on the battlefield.
The use of artificial intelligence and ground robotic systems is already changing the character of military operations, making it necessary to adapt defense plans more quickly.
Another issue will be how conventional military forces, such as infantry units and fighter jets, can support countries that possess nuclear weapons, such as the United Kingdom and the United States.
Nasima Barrow, NATO's director of nuclear policy, emphasized that conventional military support capabilities are an integral part of the defense planning process.
"Conventional support capabilities are fully part of the NDPP process. This is one of the key messages we are emphasizing ahead of the upcoming negotiations," she stated.
How will the void be filled in the event of a possible American withdrawal?
The possible reduction of the American military presence in Europe constitutes one of the greatest factors of uncertainty.
The Pentagon is expected to complete a review of the deployment of US forces on the European continent in December, just as NATO negotiations are underway.
Earlier this year, Washington withdrew several military assets, such as strategic bombers, fighter jets, drones, submarines, and warships, from the force group that could be used by the Alliance.
The upcoming American review is causing concern among European allies, as it could lead to the further withdrawal of essential assets, such as heavy transport aircraft.
The fact that the results of this review are expected in the midst of negotiations could also cause delays in the process.
Washington's push to limit its military presence in Europe will force allies to look for ways to replace American capabilities. This will open up a difficult debate about the fair sharing of the financial and military burden, at a time when national budgets are facing increasing pressure.
Camille Grand, head of the European defense industry association ASD and former senior NATO official, described the change this way:
"Until recently, the whole NATO process worked like this: you calculated what the Alliance needed, and when you found that you didn't have all the capabilities, the United States would fill the gaps."
"This is no longer valid," he added.
One of the proposals being considered is to abandon rigid requirements for certain weapons systems and replace them with operational objectives.
For example, instead of a country being required to possess a certain number of missiles, it could be assigned the mission of neutralizing Russian command centers.
This way, European allies would have more flexibility, especially those that do not have access to American weapons systems, such as Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Fabrice Pothier, former director of NATO policy planning and currently executive director of consulting firm Rasmussen Global, believes that alternatives exist.
"We don't need to have thousands of Tomahawk missiles. But we can have thousands of cheaper, lower-cost alternatives," he argued.
Geographical Disputes – Not Everyone Is Just Worried About Russia
NATO's increasing focus on the Russian threat could cause new clashes between member states, as some countries believe there are other serious security challenges.
Officially, the Alliance follows a "360-degree" security approach, according to which it must confront threats from all geographical directions.
In practice, however, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, NATO's attention has shifted significantly towards Eastern Europe.
Over the past year, attention to the north has also increased, with the creation of a mission in the Arctic, largely in response to Donald Trump's pressure regarding Greenland.
However, some allies are calling for more attention to be paid to NATO's southern and southeastern flank.
Among the issues causing concern are the presence of Russian mercenaries in Libya, the possible use of migratory flows as a tool of pressure, increased submarine activity, and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
These different priorities can complicate the process of distributing military forces and financial resources.
"There is an excessive focus on the north," commented a NATO diplomat.
"We need to redefine our priorities," he added.
More drones or more tanks? The crucial dilemma
One of the most important military dilemmas relates to the balance between new technologies and traditional weapons systems.
The war in Ukraine has highlighted the crucial role of unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous systems, which are being used on a very large scale on the battlefield.
NATO must now decide whether to give greater priority to the development and acquisition of drones or whether to continue to invest with the same intensity in conventional equipment, such as tanks and artillery.
Most member states have already drawn up plans to increase the use of unmanned systems.
The United Kingdom announced this year the creation of a "hybrid fleet", which will rely mainly on autonomous vehicles, such as the Type 93 unmanned underwater vehicles.
France has earmarked around 8,4 billion euros for drones and loitering munitions, while Germany plans to create its first regiment specialized in unmanned systems next year.
This orientation is dictated not only by technological progress, but also by the demographic challenges facing Europe.
Difficulties in recruiting new personnel into European armed forces increase the need for the use of autonomous systems.
As Camille Grand explained: “One of the reasons that is pushing everyone towards using more unmanned systems is that we have aging societies. We face human resource problems.”
At the same time, countries must find ways to keep up with Russian technological developments without draining their national defense budgets.
Admiral Pierre Vandier stated that Russia produces nine million drones per year, a figure that, according to him, requires a "quite radical effort" on the part of the Alliance.
One of the solutions he proposed is adopting a model for regularly updating military equipment, similar to a subscription service.
Such a system would enable the continuous technological renewal of weapons systems, limiting the risk of them becoming obsolete within a short time.

US NATO Illustration: Liu Rui/GT
Recently, US media outlet The Hill ran a commentary warning that the US is "on the run," citing instances including the redeployment of US bombers stationed in the UK amid security threats, the loss of military aircraft in overseas operations, and Houthi attacks against the King Khalid airport in Saudi Arabia. It also cautions that should Washington relinquish its leadership within NATO, it could be "strategically catastrophic for the alliance."
To characterize US' adjustments as "on the run" may not be entirely accurate. The US still hopes to maintain its global influence, but is increasingly reluctant to foot the bill for it. For Washington, while responsibilities can be shared with Europe, it is unwilling to relinquish its position as alliance leader.
Behind this lie real cost pressures. Long-range strikes and drone threats mean that even bases far from the front lines cannot remain unaffected. While redeploying military aircraft can reduce localized risks, it does not resolve the tension between global commitments and limited resources. With the Middle East continuing to drain military resources and Europe having its own security needs, it is difficult for the US to ensure it can address all fronts simply by increasing its budget. 
Washington is exploring new ways to share this burden. This year's US National Defense Strategy states that NATO allies should assume primary responsibility for conventional defense in Europe, with the US providing critical but more limited support. The so-called NATO 3.0 embodies this adjustment. 
However, while budgetary allocations can be increased, capabilities take years to build up. The pace at which Europe assumes responsibility for conventional defense may not necessarily keep up with the pace at which the US adjusts its deployments. If the US shortens the handover period to lighten its own burden, Europe will also have to shoulder the security risks arising from capability gaps that have not yet been filled. The "burden-sharing" thus carries the implication of shifting risks to allies ahead of time.
Europe's taking on greater responsibility for its own defense could, in principle, offer an opportunity to recalibrate US-EU relations. The crux, however, lies in how power will be distributed once these heavier burdens are assumed.
Questions over where Europe's additional defense spending will be directed, from whom military equipment will be procured, and which security needs will be prioritized all bear directly on European states' own interests. 
If the US is concerned solely with how much its allies spend, yet unwilling to accept greater autonomy for its allies in these decisions, raising defense-spending targets alone will hardly resolve such divergences. Future frictions will increasingly revolve around precisely how these funds should be spent and who gets to make those decisions.
This also points to the deeper problem laid bare by the US "on the run" anxiety. Some US strategists worry that Europe cannot sustain its security without US leadership. Yet Washington uses adjustments to its deployments as a means of exerting pressure, demanding that allies shoulder responsibilities on its terms. The signal that Europe receives is that US security commitments are subject to re-evaluation with every round of bargaining. The deeper the dependence, the greater the unease caused by this uncertainty.
The EU is advancing institutional frameworks centered on joint procurement, defense industrial capacity and defense innovation, while also adopting arrangements to streamline defense regulations and support agile and rapid defense innovation. These measures do not imply that Europe is immediately breaking away from the US, but they do demonstrate that Europe is preparing to expand its own operational capabilities.
The US is therefore forced to face an inescapable dilemma. If Europe's capabilities remain inadequate, it will be difficult for the US to truly offload its burden. However, if Europe's capabilities increase, it will inevitably be in a stronger position to discuss its own priorities. It is difficult to sustain such a relationship in the long term if one demands that Europe possess greater capabilities while expecting it to retain its previous level of deference. 
Washington may adjust its force posture and renegotiate burden-sharing arrangements, yet it cannot offload responsibilities while demanding that allies accept its arrangements unquestioningly. 
What is truly unsustainable is the self-serving desire to retain the old mode of dominance at a lower cost. Much of today's "hegemon's anxiety" in Washington stems from the growing difficulty of realizing that very ambition.

Time is running out for Ukraine…
Kyiv faces not only Russia's military pressure but also suffocating political and diplomatic pressures from its most valuable ally, the United States. Russian missiles, as even Ukrainians themselves now admit, cannot be intercepted, resulting in the systematic destruction of energy and military infrastructure in Kyiv and Odessa. A growing number of analysts point out that Ukraine will not manage to survive the coming winter.
At the same time, Ukrainian MPs in a desperate move are calling on Kyiv to "hold on" and endure for two weeks, hoping that Trump will be defeated in the November 3 midterm elections and that a shift in US political balances will positively influence developments for Kyiv. Yet reality is harsh: Ukraine is heading toward destruction, and this appears to have become evident in the West as well. As Politico characteristically reports, NATO 3.0 has already begun preparations for a war scenario with Russia.
Two more weeks
In the Ukrainian parliament, an appeal was voiced for Ukraine to endure for two more weeks, after which Kyiv expects a shift in Washington's policy. Specifically, Ukrainian MP Maryana Bezuhla estimates that ahead of the US congressional midterms, Donald Trump might intensify pressure on Kyiv, seeking to secure even a temporary halt to hostilities. Bezuhla believes Trump needs a foreign policy outcome he can present to voters as a diplomatic achievement. However, according to her, the terms of a potential agreement could prove extremely adverse for Ukraine. "We do not listen to traitors – we endure for two weeks!".
The traitors
With this appeal she addresses Ukrainians, labeling as traitors those currently in Ukraine demanding negotiations with Russia and the fastest possible achievement of peace. The Ukrainian MP ties her hopes to upcoming US elections, assessing that a potential shift in US political balances could allow Kyiv to achieve a revision of current Washington policy—essentially a return to the "Biden era." In substance, this reflects her hope for restored extensive US military support for Ukraine and a harder confrontation with Moscow. However, it must be noted that even a change in congressional composition does not automatically entail a revision of presidential decisions. American foreign policy is shaped through the interaction of many institutions, while military aid issues also depend on funding, manufacturing capabilities, and military inventory status.
Leading Ukraine to destruction
The current actions of the Ukrainian leadership are leading Ukraine to destruction in a war it cannot win, stated retired US Army lieutenant colonel Daniel Davis. "Let us consider what is about to happen. Do you imagine they will somehow manage to maintain their defensive positions along the contact line while Russia continues advancing until at some point it tires of war? Let us use logic: Ukraine has been left without air defense, cannot maintain economic activity, and relies entirely on external funding," Davis underlined, pointing out that the Ukrainian people ought to protest against the top political leadership that allowed the country to fall into such a state of decline across all sectors. Concurrently, he added that Europeans ought to focus their attention on events within their own countries instead of continuing to satisfy Zelensky's demands. "What they are doing is madness! It makes absolutely no sense," Davis concluded.
Kyiv unprotected
Russia launched two ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv over the past 24 hours, and in both instances, Ukrainian air defense failed to react effectively, underlined Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat. The Air Force of the Ukrainian Armed Forces confirmed that the Americans failed to notify them regarding the launch of Russian ballistic missiles against Kyiv, though clarifying this occurred on Sunday night during the initial strike on the Ukrainian capital. The missiles were detected by radar when already approaching Kyiv, leaving insufficient time for reaction. During the second attack, the US sent a warning regarding the launches, but with a delay. This offered little practical help to Ukrainian air defense, leaving minimal reaction time. Consequently, air raid sirens activated after the strike had already occurred. Yuriy Ihnat stated: "Our specialists, cooperating with American partners, are investigating the reasons why this specific intelligence was not transmitted. If we have this intelligence beforehand, even a few minutes early—for example five minutes—then naturally this is very useful. However, sometimes information arrives with a very significant delay." Through these remarks, Ihnat confirmed that no successful ballistic missile interception took place overnight, despite Americans ultimately transmitting launch intelligence during the second attack.
Hell in Odessa
Russians continue executing strikes against targets in Ukraine. During the night from Saturday to Sunday, October 18, Geran-type strike unmanned aerial vehicles were deployed, alongside reports regarding the use of Banderol and Dan-T systems. Primary nighttime strikes occurred in the Odessa region, while attacks were also recorded in Zaporizhzhia and the Rivne region. In the Odessa region, Geran drones struck an electrical power substation in the area between Artsyz and Tatarbunary. Following the attack, a major fire broke out at the facilities, while the southern part of the region was left without electricity. Ukrainian energy company DTEK acknowledges power supply problems in the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Izmail, and Bolhrad areas, but maintains these constitute "local damage."
Politico: NATO prepares for war
And while Ukraine's end is deemed certain, the West is beginning to openly examine the scenario of conflict with Russia. According to Politico, NATO is initiating negotiations regarding the military forces and weapon systems that would be required in the event of a potential war with Russia. Alliance nations are set to discuss establishing defense capability targets for 2029, a year presented as the likely timeframe for military confrontation. As reported, NATO will need to address 5 key issues ahead of potential conflict with Russia. Initially, NATO nations must define their "level of ambition" and determine the precise number of troops and military capabilities allies are prepared to commit in the event of war. Historically, NATO allies agreed that beyond forces required for major military operations, they must maintain 18 additional brigades, each comprising approximately 5,000 troops. These forces are earmarked for smaller crisis-management missions outside Alliance territory, such as those in Afghanistan or Kosovo.
NATO 3.0
However, US pressure for European allies to assume a greater share of responsibility for their own security—an approach termed "NATO 3.0"—could lead to reducing or even completely abolishing requirements for such smaller operations. Discussions will also examine whether the defense planning process itself should be accelerated in the future to match the blistering pace of technological innovations on battlefields, from artificial intelligence to ground robotics systems. Allies are further expected to examine how they can provide conventional military support—such as ground forces or aircraft—to nuclear-armed countries like the UK and the US. "Conventional support capabilities undeniably form part of the NDPP process," stated Nassima Barrows, NATO nuclear policy director. "This constitutes a core message we emphasize ahead of the next round of negotiations."
Replenishing losses
Subsequently, the Alliance must examine how to replenish military capabilities that might be lost, given Washington's intention to curtail its military presence in Europe. Looming over these talks is the Pentagon's impending review of American force presence in Europe. Washington already withdrew assets earlier this year including strategic bombers, fighter jets, drones, submarines, and warships from forces available for NATO use. The Pentagon assessment is scheduled for completion in December—meaning while NATO negotiations are already underway—prompting concerns that the process may be delayed. Fears also persist that the US could withdraw military assets essential to Europe, such as heavy transport aircraft. Washington's effort to curtail its military presence in Europe will compel allies to urgently seek ways of replacing American capabilities. This will open discussions on burden-sharing, expected to prove exceptionally difficult as national budgets face mounting pressures. "Until recently, the entire NATO process functioned as follows: you calculated what the Alliance needed, and when you found you lacked necessary means, the US covered the gaps," stated Camille Grand, head of European defense industry association ASD and former high-ranking NATO official.
"This no longer applies"
One way to address the problem would involve transitioning from specific weapon system requirements to establishing operational targets for each country, such as capability to neutralize Russian command positions. Such an approach could offer greater flexibility to European allies lacking access to US weapon systems like Tomahawk cruise missiles. "We do not need to possess thousands of Tomahawk missiles. But we can possess thousands of cheaper, low-cost alternatives," stated Fabrice Pothier, former NATO policy planning director and current managing director of consultancy Rasmussen Global.

articles.title: A Better “America First”
articles.summary: Charles Kupchan, who served in the Clinton and Obama administrations, argues that many aspects of Trump's foreign policy are worth keeping and align with changes in the international system. He explains how the next president can marry the good impulses of "America first" with the best of liberal internationalism.
articles.full_text:
Critics from across the political spectrum have disparaged U.S. President Donald Trump’s “America first” brand of statecraft—and for good reason. He has alienated allies, appeased great-power rivals, launched yet another failed war of choice in the Middle East, and blundered into trade wars that have worsened the United States’ affordability crisis.
But as debate heats up about what the next administration’s foreign policy should look like, Democrats and Republicans alike must be careful not to throw the baby out with the bathwater. Trump is right to recognize that U.S. strategy is in need of an overhaul. Most of his instincts are sound and align with fundamental changes in the international system and in American public opinion. His “America first” foreign policy is a symptom, not a cause, of global disarray and the public’s turn against the establishment; many U.S. voters have been disillusioned by the country’s chronic overreach abroad and the affordability crisis at home. Trump successfully tapped into these grievances by promising to scale back international entanglements and bring back factories and manufacturing jobs.
These are worthy goals, but Trump’s policies have badly missed their mark. He has started new wars and mostly failed to end old ones, and his tariffs have fueled inflation while doing little to resuscitate the manufacturing sector. Trump has implemented his course corrections with marked incompetence, making policy by impulse, gutting the diplomatic corps, relying on an inexperienced inner circle, and prizing loyalty over fact.
The challenge ahead is not to reflexively restore what came before; liberal internationalism long served the United States well, but during an era that no longer exists. Instead of burying “America first,” Trump’s successor should salvage its best elements and implement them more capably. The next version of U.S. foreign policy should marry the realist impulses that shape “America first” with the liberal cause that remains at the heart of the American experience. That composite strategy would see Washington pare back its commitments abroad, reach across ideological dividing lines to work with great-power rivals, operate through nimble coalitions, and repair the United States’ broken social contract and ailing democracy. Foreign policy starts at home: only by redressing the socioeconomic discontent that has cleaved the body politic into hostile camps can the country recoup the bipartisan centrism and democratic vitality needed to anchor a purposeful and steady statecraft.
OUT OF THE MIRE
Two tectonic shifts are leading to a historic turning point. Power is rapidly shifting from West to East and North to South, as Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, and other large developing countries rise. The United States and its democratic allies, assuming they manage to stay partners, will remain an influential bloc, but no longer a preponderant one. As the diffusion of power fuels geopolitical rivalries, Americans are growing weary of entanglement in a fragmenting world. Meanwhile, technological advances made possible by the digital age have undermined the social contract of the industrial era and hollowed out the middle class. As broadly shared prosperity has given way to economic insecurity and inequality, political cleavages have emerged along socioeconomic, educational, and rural-urban lines. Liberal democracy is in retreat worldwide, including in the United States, where the centrist, bipartisan compact that long anchored U.S. statecraft has collapsed.
Enter Trump. By the time U.S. forces withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021, more than 70 percent of Americans deemed the two-decade war a failure. Speaking to an electorate fed up with the never-ending conflicts in the Middle East, Trump pledged “no more wars” as he ran for reelection in 2024. He began his second term by using force sparingly. The single-night air campaign against Iran’s nuclear installations in June 2025 and the in-and-out raid to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026 succeeded in their narrow aims. Perhaps emboldened by these low-cost wins, Trump then proceeded to launch a full-scale war against Iran in February 2026. By planning for a short conflict and getting stuck in a long one, he fell into the very trap that he swore to avoid.
Given that the United States keeps getting mired in errant conflicts, Congress urgently needs to reassert its constitutional obligation to approve acts of war and oversee retrenchment. The bar for engaging in major conflicts outside the core strategic areas of Europe and East Asia should be quite high. It is past time for Washington to return to its traditional geopolitical vocation: playing the role of great-power balancer in order to preserve stability in the strategic heartland. American strategy toward Europe and East Asia has been a steady and cost-effective success, facilitating great-power peace since 1945. The roughly 150,000 U.S. troops still stationed in these core theaters are a wise investment in extending that track record.
 Power is rapidly shifting from West to East and North to South.
A retrenchment from the Middle East and other peripheral areas does not mean a comprehensive retreat, but it does mean relying far more heavily on diplomacy and economic engagement than on the military. When force is required to counter threats to U.S. interests or allies, the United States should generally limit itself to supporting regional partners and relying on special forces and surgical strikes. As it seeks to end its addiction to military force, Washington could take a page from Beijing: China has spread its influence and maximized its leverage in the global South not through armed intervention but through investments, trade, and the Belt and Road Initiative, the biggest infrastructure project in modern history.
As the United States refocuses its attention and resources on maintaining stability in Asia and Europe, it can nonetheless lighten its load by rebalancing its alliances. Trump made headway by pushing allies to shoulder their fair share of the defense burden; NATO members and Asian allies are substantially increasing their defense budgets. But true to form, Trump has marred this success by taking actions that corrode decades of trust, such as threatening to seize Greenland and repeatedly demeaning allied leaders.
Allies are force multipliers; rather than alienating them, the United States should hold them even closer as they beef up their militaries. Washington should work with allies’ defense industries and military planners to come up with a new division of labor, set force levels, and create a realistic timetable to meet their goals. The United States’ network of defense pacts is poised to get stronger as its allies get stronger, but only if rebalancing occurs with consent, foresight, and respectful treatment of partners.
SPHERE FACTOR
Adjusting U.S. strategy to the onset of multipolarity also entails building on Trump’s recognition that regional spheres of influence are making a comeback. As power diffuses across the international system, Washington will be neither willing nor able to oversee all the world’s main strategic theaters. Instead, major powers in each theater will play a more prominent role in guiding projects of regional integration, shaping regional order, and providing public goods.
For decades, most American policymakers have denounced spheres of influence. In 2021, Secretary of State Antony Blinken called the concept “a recipe for an international system that falls apart.” Yet since the founding era, the United States has prioritized establishing and defending its own sphere of influence in the Western Hemisphere. During the Cold War, Washington granted the Soviet Union a buffer zone in Eastern Europe while entrenching its own zones of control in Western Europe, Northeast Asia, and the Middle East.
Trump recognizes this double standard. The 2025 National Security Strategy endorses a reassertion of U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere and calls on other countries to “assume primary responsibility for their regions.” Trump has exhibited long overdue regard for the strategic interests of other great powers and appropriate caution about the extension of U.S. commitments into their backyards. He has precluded the possibility of Ukraine’s entry into NATO, aware that membership would run afoul of Russia’s legitimate security interests and overextend the alliance. He is also looking for ways to reduce tensions in East Asia, pausing arms sales to Taiwan and canceling military exercises with South Korea.
 When the United States defects, others follow. 
But even if Trump is right to herald a return of spheres of influence, he has acted with self-defeating excess. In the Western Hemisphere, he has been driving away Canada, treating Venezuela like a U.S. colony, strangling Cuba, ordering strikes of questionable legality against boats allegedly running drugs, and renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario. Instead of working toward a benign sphere of influence that attracts neighbors and promotes stability, Trump has been building a malign sphere of coercion that prompts other countries to run for cover.
Trump is making a similar mess in other theaters. Even if he is right to close NATO’s door to Ukraine, he has failed to convince Russia to end its war of aggression. A vision of a stable security order in Europe is nowhere to be found. And although regional integration offers the best bet for creating the stronger Europe that Trump seeks, he is backing far-right parties hostile to the European Union. Trump’s approach to East Asia is similarly muddled. articles.title: Europe’s Credibility Gap
articles.summary: Ngaire Woods, Dean of Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government, Claas Mertens, also at Oxford, have written a piece arguing that Europe, despite its attempts at self-sufficiency, remains dependent on an unpredictable United States. The continent needs to address this vulnerability so that it can convince other countries, many of which find themselves similarly vulnerable to great-power coercion, that it is a worthy partner.
articles.full_text:
The second Trump administration’s National Security Strategy declared that “the days of the United States propping up the entire world order like Atlas are over.” That sentiment has animated much of the administration’s foreign policy over the past two years, and its approach to Europe has been no exception. In 2025, the United States suspended military aid to Ukraine, and in May of this year, it announced it would remove 5,000 troops from Germany. President Donald Trump has threatened to seize Greenland, the territory of a fellow NATO country, and promised to levy tariffs against member states that opposed the effort. When the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, they neither consulted nor warned European powers, which have been left to face the war’s economic consequences largely alone.
Europe has not stood idly by amid this onslaught. It stepped in to fill the gaps left by the United States’ withdrawal of financial support for Ukraine in 2025. During the Greenland episode, European countries facing tariffs convinced Trump to back down by threatening massive retaliatory trade measures against the United States. And the continent has begun to deepen its other relationships. The EU has set up a $168 billion defense-loan scheme, with Canada as its first non-European member. Earlier this year, it finalized the largest trade agreement in its history, with India, and signed a long-delayed deal with the South American economic bloc Mercosur.
These measures have been encouraging departures from the bureaucratic indecisiveness for which the EU has frequently been criticized. But despite its leaders’ newfound interest in self-sufficiency, Europe remains dependent on the United States. In fact, some of its attempts to stand on its own have made it more dependent on the United States. European defense planning, command, nuclear deterrence, and military enabling systems still rely on American capabilities. Increased defense spending buys American weapons. As of 2025, the United States supplied more than half of the EU’s liquefied natural gas imports. Many of the continent’s most promising technology firms still move to New York or San Francisco.
This continued dependence has in turn weakened Europe’s credibility with other countries seeking new security, technology, and economic ties of their own. For decades, the European offer to these countries relied on the continent’s relationship with Washington. As long as the United States underwrote European security and welcomed Europe’s integration with its economy, that offer was an attractive one. Now that Washington has begun to treat both arrangements as negotiable, however, it no longer is. The weaker the transatlantic relationship becomes, the more Europe needs other countries’ export markets, raw materials, defense industrial capacity, and solidarity against coercion—and the less able it is to convince those countries of its worth as a partner. Europe needs a better offer, grounded in its own capabilities rather than those of its mercurial ally.
OFFER EXPIRED
European countries have long presented themselves as leaders on issues such as the environment, consumer protection, and high regulatory standards. To neighboring countries, Europe dangled membership in and association with the EU. Beyond the continent, it promised developmental and humanitarian partnerships in the form of aid through the EU and national agencies. Until recently, these were appealing terms: 13 countries have joined the EU since 2004, and more than 140 countries accepted some form of aid from EU or member state programs.
The United States upheld the underlying security and economic order that made these offers possible. EU aspirants could count on Washington to underwrite Europe’s defense through NATO, and and non-European countries could count on a U.S.-led rules-based economic order, within which they could easily access European aid, markets, and investment.
But the U.S. retrenchment has accelerated the emergence of a more bellicose “might is right” disorder in which different needs have risen to the fore. Countries are now seeking security partnerships to shore up their defense capabilities, stable trade relationships to protect against economic warfare, and financing to make up for cuts in aid and increases in the costs of government borrowing.
For example, when Ukraine turned to Europe in the early 2010s, it did so because of the prosperity and modernization that economic integration promised. But Kyiv now needs intelligence and weapons to fend off Russia, which Europe can deliver only through the United States. For countries similarly seeking security assistance and cooperation, dependence on such a fickle partner is a liability.
Partners hit by Trump’s tariffs need access to reliable markets to export goods and services once destined for the United States. But Europe has felt the need to defend its own economies instead of opening up its markets to them. For instance, the European Commission drastically increased tariffs on steel and reduced its quotas for duty-free imports, blocking India, South Korea, and Turkey from selling into the European market—precisely as those countries were searching for alternative markets to the United States.
 Europe has the potential to present partners with a more compelling offer.
Other countries need financing for infrastructure and the energy transition. Europe has the firepower to meet these countries’ needs, but its commitments take far too long to be realized as completed projects. And as in security, the U.S. withdrawal has left Europe adrift. Joint G-7 packages to finance clean energy buildouts in Indonesia, South Africa, and Vietnam, for example, suffered when Washington withdrew its support in 2025.
Europe has lately shown some ability to rise to the occasion. In 2025, EU member states’ combined annual military expenditure was approximately $461 billion, less than the United States’ $954 billion, but higher than China’s $336 billion and Russia’s $190 billion. When the United States wound down its aid to Ukraine in 2025, European governments made up most of the shortfall and have since committed to financing Kyiv’s war effort through 2027. The continent also has an existing defense industrial base, two permanent UN Security Council seats, and nuclear forces. Partners just beyond the core add more: Ukraine has a battle-tested army and an innovative drone industry, and Turkey has NATO’s second-largest army and access to the strategically important Black and Mediterranean Seas.
There is similar cause for optimism in trade and finance. The EU’s 2026 trade agreement with India removed nearly all tariffs for both parties, reduced nontariff barriers to trade, and made it easier for Indians and Europeans to temporarily work in each other’s markets. The EU’s Global Gateway investment program, Europe’s answer to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, passed its $335 billion mobilization target ahead of schedule.
These individual successes show that Europe has the potential to present partners with a more compelling offer. Yet much of that potential remains unfulfilled.
THE AGONY OF SELF-DEFEAT
Europe has substantial assets across security, trade, and finance, but it lacks the internal cohesion needed to bundle them into a comprehensive package to attract other countries and bolster its own autonomy. When Europe could fall back on the United States’ leadership in institutions such as the World Trade Organization and NATO, internal disunity was less of a problem: American military commanders not only supported but organized European defense, and U.S.-backed rules governing global trade opened foreign markets to European exports, reducing the need to negotiate bilateral agreements. Without that leadership, the continent has been left to overcome its internal fragmentation on its own.
Nowhere is that fragmentation more apparent than on security. European leaders have committed to improving the continent’s defense in response to Washington’s wavering on NATO, but defense budgets, industries, and forces remain primarily national. As governments prioritize negotiating the best deals for domestic firms and other constituencies, conflicts arise: joint projects fail, purchases overlap, redundant R & D efforts waste precious resources. These frustrations have ultimately led the continent to simply purchase more U.S. systems. The EU’s Security Action for Europe loan program aims to reverse this trend by financing member states’ joint purchases of European equipment. But loans alone will neither overcome distributional conflicts nor create common command structures, standards, and logistics.
Europe does negotiate its trade deals with one voice. But many agreements need to be ratified in each country, leaving them at the mercy of domestic lobbies, from farmers to automakers, which seek to protect their markets at the expense of the continent’s collective interest. More than a decade after Canada and the EU negotiated the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, for example, just 17 of the organization’s 27 member states have ratified it. The 2026 trade deal with Mercosur, in the works for decades, was immediately contested, politically and legally, by individual member states and their representatives in the European Parliament.
On finance, Europe does not lack money but channels it through a byzantine set of EU instruments, member-state agencies, development banks, and changing flagship initiatives. Partners are left to navigate this morass of funding sources, each with their own procedures, timelines, and conditions. In Ghana, for example, Europe is present through EU programming, member-state development agencies, the European Investment Bank, and Global Gateway initiatives.
